name: Punchmole
popularity: 19 stars, 4 forks, 1 watcher. Author states it has been used 'extensively for heavy-duty websocket applications' and deployed on Kubernetes with 20 replicas handling thousands of req/s, but no widespread public adoption evidenced (no notable dependents listed on GitHub).
maturity: 46 commits total, single-maintainer project (degola). README describes it as 'experimental for quite a while' but claims real production use. No tagged releases visible in the extracted page; no CI badges found. Small commit count and single-author project are mild red flags for long-term maintenance, though the code is simple/small (low surface area to break).
client_requirements: No TAP/TUN interfaces, no admin/root privileges. Pure Node.js WebSocket client — install via `npm install -g punchmole` and run `punchmole` configured entirely via env vars (PUNCHMOLE_API_KEY, DOMAIN, TARGET_URL, PUNCHMOLE_ENDPOINT_URL). It is explicitly importable as a library: `import { PunchmoleClient } from 'punchmole'` and called as a function that returns an EventEmitter (registered/request/request-end events) inside your own Node.js process — meaning for a Node.js host app it can be embedded directly with zero external process/binary needed at all, which is even simpler than a CLI/binary requirement.
server_requirements: Server source is fully available in the same repo (PunchmoleServer.js, server.js, app.js). It is a single HTTP port that upgrades to WebSocket, forwarding requests by Host header to the matching connected client. Deployable via npm global install, Docker, or Kubernetes manifest included in repo. Critically, it also exposes a programmatic Node.js embedding API: `import { PunchmoleServer } from 'punchmole'; PunchmoleServer(PORT, API_KEYS, PATH, logger)` — this can be mounted inside an existing Node/Express-style app rather than only run as a standalone binary.
has_programmable_api: true — JavaScript/Node.js. Both PunchmoleServer() and PunchmoleClient() are plain importable functions/EventEmitters usable directly inside a host Node.js process (e.g., embed the server logic inside a SvelteKit/Node backend and programmatically register domains/API keys via env-var-equivalent function args), though this is an in-process embed rather than a separate HTTP REST control-plane for remote registration.
viability_notes: Meets all hard client constraints (no TUN/TAP, no root, trivial npm install or embeddable JS import) and the server is a small self-hostable Node.js WebSocket proxy with source available and a clean programmatic JS API for both client and server. Main risk is small community/maintainer bus-factor (19 stars, single author) and the lack of a dedicated REST control-plane (registration is via API keys/env vars or direct function calls rather than a management HTTP API), so our SvelteKit app would need to call the Node functions in-process or shell out to configure it rather than hit a REST endpoint.

name: hsync
popularity: 15 stars, 6 forks, 5 watchers. Published on npm (badge present) with a companion server package hsync-server; no other notable adoption/dependents surfaced.
maturity: 98 commits, active CI (GitHub Actions badge passing), has husky/eslint/vitest tooling and even an llms.txt file suggesting recent modernization — indicates ongoing maintenance rather than an abandoned prototype. No explicit last-commit date surfaced in the extracted page, but tooling (vitest, eslint flat config) suggests a fairly recent, actively-tended codebase.
client_requirements: No TAP/TUN interfaces, no admin/root privileges. Install via `npm i -g hsync` or run with `npx hsync`, or even load directly in a browser via a CDN `<script>` tag creating a global `hsync` object with `hsync.dynamicConnect()`. This is a plain WebSocket-based reverse-proxy client, not actually a WebRTC/P2P NAT-punching tool for the core proxy path (the task brief's claim of WebRTC P2P forwarding was not confirmed in the README — hsync's documented mechanism is a WebSocket connection to an hsync-server relay, plus TCP tunneling between two hsync clients through the server). No admin rights or complex install needed either way.
server_requirements: The client repo itself does not bundle the server; it depends on a separate project, hsync-server (https://github.com/monteslu/hsync-server), which is presumably also Node.js given the ecosystem, but its source/API details were not directly fetched in this pass. hsync is configured via CLI flags/env vars (HSYNC_SERVER, HSYNC_SECRET, port/relay options) to point at a self-hosted or the public hsync.tech relay. No confirmed embeddable server-side JS API or REST control-plane was found without inspecting hsync-server directly.
server_language: JavaScript (Node.js) — hsync-server is a separate repo, presumed Node given the client is Node/browser-only; not independently verified in this pass.
has_programmable_api: Partially true — JavaScript. The client is programmable/embeddable (browser global object, `dynamicConnect()`, Node module usage via cli.js/index.js), but a server-side embeddable API / REST control-plane was NOT verified since hsync-server is a separate unreviewed repo.
viability_notes: Client-side is fully compliant with our hard constraints (no TUN/TAP, no root, simple npm/npx install, even browser-embeddable) and is a genuinely lightweight Node/WebSocket reverse-proxy. However the server component lives in a separate repo (hsync-server) that wasn't directly verified for source availability or a programmatic control-plane API, so it scores lower than Punchmole until that gap is closed by follow-up research.

name: netmask
popularity: 14 stars, 2 forks, 1 watcher — a small hobby-scale project with no evidence of notable adoption.
maturity: Only 5 commits total; roadmap items (Automatic TLS, HTTP control panel, GUI kill-connection) are still unchecked/unimplemented. This is an early-stage, likely single-author side project with minimal commit history — a clear red flag for production reliability and long-term maintenance.
client_requirements: DISQUALIFYING for our use case: the client (netmaskc) ships with a GUI interface by default; a `--nogui` flag exists to run headless, so a no-GUI mode is technically available. However it requires Python 3.6+ installed plus `pip install netmask` or manual setup.py install, and operates as a raw TCP/UDP-level tunneling tool (binds arbitrary local ports across an encrypted stream with a shared 'communication key') rather than an HTTP/WebSocket reverse tunnel with subdomain routing — a materially different architecture than what we need. No TAP/TUN kernel interfaces or root are indicated, but the tool's low commit count, GUI-first design, and lack of an HTTP control-plane (explicitly listed as a future roadmap item, unimplemented) make it a poor fit.
server_requirements: Server (netmasks) source is available in the same repo; runs as a Python script/binary with --port/--key/--verbose flags binding to IPv4/IPv6 listeners. No HTTP control panel exists yet — the README's own roadmap lists 'Control panel for server (HTTP)' as an unchecked, unimplemented future feature. No JS/TS server library exists since the whole project is Python.
has_programmable_api: false — no HTTP/REST control-plane exists; it's explicitly on the unimplemented roadmap. No JS/TS server API of any kind (project is pure Python).
viability_notes: Disqualified primarily by its GUI-centric client design and by the complete absence of a control-plane/API (still just a roadmap item), plus a very thin commit history (5 commits) signaling an unfinished, unmaintained hobby project. It's also a low-level TCP/UDP port-forwarder rather than an HTTP tunnel with domain/subdomain routing, making it architecturally mismatched to our reverse-HTTP-tunnel use case regardless of the GUI concern.

name: ephemeral-hidden-service
popularity: 10 stars, 2 forks, 1 watcher — very small, niche utility with no notable adoption signals.
maturity: Only 3 commits total in the entire repo history — essentially a minimal, likely one-off script-level project. No releases, no CI badges visible. This is a strong red flag for maintenance/production-readiness; it reads as a small personal utility rather than an actively maintained tunneling solution.
client_requirements: Heavy overhead relative to our constraints: requires a full local Tor installation and a running Tor daemon with its controller port accessible (and optionally a hashed controller password). No TAP/TUN virtual interface is needed and no explicit root/admin requirement was stated for running the Python script itself, BUT standing up and maintaining a local Tor process is itself a non-trivial, heavyweight dependency (a full onion-routing client, not a simple lightweight tunnel binary) — this is exactly the kind of 'complex install' overhead we want to avoid, even though technically it's just `pip install`/`pipx install` for the wrapper script.
server_requirements: There is no 'server' component in the traditional reverse-tunnel sense — the Tor network itself acts as the rendezvous/relay layer, and the 'server' side is simply the Tor hidden-service descriptor published to the Tor network. There is no self-hosted control-plane, REST API, or JS/TS server library — the entire tool is a thin Python CLI wrapper (`ephemeral-hidden-service --local-port ... --hidden-service-port ...`) around the Tor control protocol (stem-like control-port automation).
server_language: N/A — no custom server; relies on the Tor network/daemon itself (Tor is written in C).
has_programmable_api: false — no HTTP/REST control-plane and no JS/TS API of any kind; it's a pure Python CLI wrapper around Tor's controller protocol.
viability_notes: Fails our requirements on multiple fronts: it mandates installing and running a full Tor daemon (heavy, non-trivial overhead well beyond a 'simple package-manager install'), provides no programmable server API or control-plane we could hit from SvelteKit, and the repo itself is barely maintained (3 commits, 10 stars). Onion-service latency/reliability is also generally much worse than a dedicated WebSocket tunnel for a hosted-inference use case.

name: TunnelAPI 1.0
license: Proprietary (NOT open source) — repo LICENSE file is titled 'API Response Manager - Proprietary License', explicitly forbids public redistribution, commercial use, and using the software to compete with the author's own commercial offerings, without a separate agreement. Verified: the repo at vijaypurohit322/api-response-manager is indeed the source for tunnelapi.in (README states 'TunnelAPI: Secure tunneling and API collaboration platform' and links to tunnelapi.in directly), but it fails the 'open source, reasonably permissive license' hard requirement entirely.
language: JavaScript/Node.js (backend, tunnel-server, tunnel-client, frontend all JS-based per repo folder structure); uses MongoDB for metadata.
popularity: 7 stars, 3 forks, 1 watcher — very small/early project; published as an npm package 'api-response-manager' with npm version/downloads badges, but no evidence of significant adoption.
maturity: 66 commits; has GitHub Actions CI, a CHANGELOG.md, and versioned releases (v2.0.3 theme referenced) suggesting active recent development. Tunnel feature explicitly documented as 'Phase 1 Complete' / 'Version 1.0.0 (Phase 1 - MVP)', 'Status: Development/Testing' as of a November 2025 doc update — i.e., the tunneling capability itself is brand-new/MVP-stage, not battle-tested.
client_requirements: No TAP/TUN interfaces or root/admin required. Tunnel client is a plain Node.js script (`node client.js <tunnelId> <subdomain> <localPort> <authToken> <userId>`) run via `npm install` in a `tunnel-client` folder — simple enough, though it requires cloning/running from the monorepo rather than a single standalone binary or `npm install -g` global package (adds minor friction vs. Punchmole/hsync).
server_requirements: Full source available (backend, tunnel-server, tunnel-client, frontend, proxy, mongo-init in one monorepo) — but usage is gated by the proprietary license which explicitly disallows using it to build/host a competing commercial/SaaS product or redistributing modified deployments, making it legally unsuitable for our hosted-server use case regardless of technical fit. It does expose a real HTTP/REST control-plane: POST /api/tunnels (create, with subdomain/rateLimit/auth options), GET /api/tunnels (list), GET /api/tunnels/:id/stats, DELETE /api/tunnels/:id, GET /api/tunnels/check/:subdomain — all JWT-authenticated Express-style JSON endpoints, which is exactly the kind of programmatic registration API our SvelteKit app would want.
server_language: JavaScript (Node.js) — backend (Express + MongoDB), tunnel-server (WebSocket + HTTP reverse proxy), tunnel-client all Node.js.
has_programmable_api: true — JavaScript/Node.js REST API (JWT-authenticated Express endpoints under /api/tunnels for create/list/stats/delete/subdomain-check), plus a requirable tunnel-client module. Technically the best-matching control-plane of all 5 candidates, but rendered moot by the license.
viability_notes: Ironically the closest technical match to our control-plane wishlist (full REST API for tunnel CRUD, JS/Node server, no TUN/root on the client) but is disqualified outright by license: the repo is proprietary, explicitly prohibits commercial/competing use and redistribution, and requires a separate commercial agreement for any hosted/SaaS use — incompatible with the task's hard 'open source, permissive license' requirement. Also very early-stage (Phase 1 MVP, Nov 2025, 7 stars) even setting licensing aside.
